posts.caption: My husband found the feed receipt on the kitchen counter and read it twice, the way you read a restaurant bill when the waiter says market price. She watched the whole thing through the window over the sink, ears forward, chewing a mouthful of hay she had absolutely not been given. He said her name in a flat voice. She blinked at him, slowly. By evening he had carried her a flake of the good alfalfa and a warm bucket, grumbling the whole walk across the yard. I counted it as a draw. She counted it as a win, and she is usually right about these things.
posts.first: He still insists he has no favorite, but I've watched him sneak her a peppermint behind the hay shed when he thinks I'm in the house. Last winter he bought her a heated bucket and never mentioned it. I found out from the receipt. We have a lot of receipts around here.

posts.caption: The tag on the new blanket promised it would shed rain, snow, and wind, and I believed every word for the eleven minutes it took to buckle the belly straps over her feathers. Big Red does not hold still for belly straps. The second I had them fastened, the sky opened over the paddock and she walked straight to the deepest puddle on the property to stand in it. I stood at the gate with a towel and a very quiet opinion. When I peeled the blanket off at dark, it was dry underneath and caked with mud on top. The manufacturer was technically right.
posts.first: My grandmother hung her barn blankets on a nail by the door, and every one of them smelled like wet dog and cedar. I can't get that smell out of mine either. I quit trying around the third winter. It smells like her barn now, and Big Red doesn't mind a bit.

posts.quote: A round bale is supposed to last eleven days. The horse believes it lasts until he can see the ground.
posts.first: The hay man unloaded forty bales last week and stacked them in the exact order I'd asked him not to. I thanked him anyway. Then I restacked everything after dark, by flashlight, while the horse supervised from the fence.

posts.caption: The water bucket had a skin of ice at 6:10, and I knew before I opened the stall door what kind of day it was going to be. Homebody hadn't moved from the corner where I left her the night before, the barn cat still curled on her back like a hot water bottle. I broke the ice, carried out the steaming bran mash in the green bucket, and she lifted her head exactly two inches. That was the whole greeting, and it was plenty. I stood in the aisle a while with my hands around the warm bucket. The chores did not agree with me.
posts.first: I keep a quilt over her stall door from November through March. It started as a draft stopper and became a tradition without anyone voting. She sniffs it every evening before she goes in, the way you check your own pillow. I wash it twice a season and she has never once complained.

posts.caption: The bell came home in the feed store bag by accident. I'd gone in for two bags of senior pellets and came out with a small brass bell the clerk swore was free. It hung on his stall door for three days before anyone noticed. Now it rings whenever he shifts his weight, and he has shifted his weight a great deal. He is twenty-six and has never once been a fidgeter. I think he likes having a sound that belongs to him. I've stopped telling him it was a mistake.
posts.first: My father kept an old gray gelding, soft in the lip and white around the eyes. Dad hummed to him at dusk while he cleaned the stall, never a real song. I caught myself doing it yesterday. The Old Timer lifted one ear and kept chewing. I took that as a good review.

posts.caption: The trailer had been hitched since seven, and the plan was simple: wait by the ramp. Pudding is very good at plans that end in a snack. I turned around to check the hitch lights, and when I looked back he had walked twelve feet to the grain bin, which sits close enough to the trailer that he can argue the point. One ear was in the lid and the other was tracking my footsteps. I didn't have the heart. We left twenty minutes late and the show was fine. He smelled like sweet feed the whole ride home.
posts.first: My first pony did the same thing at every show I ever took her to. I'd lose her at the concession stand and find her at the feed tent, calmly eating oats out of somebody's upturned hat. I paid for the oats every time. Some habits you just inherit.
